First, we express

$$
f(x)=(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{2}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=2u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =2u\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=3\operatorname{sec}⁡u,\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=3\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡u\operatorname{tan}⁡u\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-3(1)(1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =-3x+\frac{3\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
